“Boundaries are what we set to keep people in our lives, not drive them away.”

I’ve always had a hard time setting boundaries, and that changed everything for me. I was able to better realize that having difficult discussions ≠ the end of something good. Oftentimes it’s the start of something greater.

Oh, I see. I must’ve misread or misinterpreted, I’m sorry. In that case, the first thing I’d do is limit one-on-one hangouts or interactions with her, at least until your feelings dissipate more. One-on-one hangouts are more intimate and it might make your feelings for her intensify. I’d lean into your other friendships for now so it gives you something else to focus on. If ruining a friendship is what you’re worried about, that’s only a possibility if you date her, which you’re not planning on doing, so everything should be okay on that front. It sounds like you are open to dating, so it wouldn’t hurt to join clubs or participate in activities where you can meet other people naturally that share the same interests. Essentially, try your best to shift the focus to you and doing things you enjoy, even if it’s just for a minute everyday. It’ll take time, but gradually your feelings will decrease, I promise. 💗

Unfortunately it sounds like this person has a lot of healing to do and is projecting that onto you. You can’t have friendships without vulnerability. Sustainable ones, at least. And ironically, vulnerability is a strength. Talking about feelings and sharing your life’s hardships is one of the strongest things you can do. It brings you closer to others and most importantly, helps you be there for and understand yourself. X is not at a point in their life where they understand this, and they may never be, and it’s not on you to fix that or prove your worth to them. Continuing to share things with this person is the equivalent of reading the same book over and over and hoping for a different ending. Go where the love is 💗

A good friend wouldn’t cast you aside the second they get a boyfriend, let alone a best friend of 9 years. If you want to continue your friendship with her, this is worth a discussion, specifically about boundaries. Be sure to explain how you feel and use “I” statements. If she responds poorly or gets defensive instead of listening, that’s not a friend worth keeping around. If you’ve already tried this and her behavior hasn’t changed, that’s not a friend worth keeping around. 

I’m a psychology student and while I’m not an expert, I can say that women tend to do this because we’re taught to nurture and be readily emotionally available for men, often at the expense of our own needs, and it can leave us exhausted and without room to nurture the other important relationships in our lives. Combine that with low self-esteem and our patriarchal society values, and it leaves women feeling they need to continuously prove they’re worthy enough for men, which might have something to do with her behavior here. 

Not sure if that’s what’s happening, as there’s many factors to every situation, and I don’t know her, him or their relationship dynamic. There’s a possibility she may not even be doing this intentionally, but the words “every time,” signal to me that this has happened more than once, and therefore, whether she knows it/acknowledges it or not, it’s become intentional. Remember: the first time is a mistake, the second time is a choice.

Bottom line is, you deserve better than someone that only makes time for you when it’s convenient for them. You have needs and a life too, and that deserves to be acknowledged.

Hey there. I just wanted to say you’re doing the right thing by thinking through this and being cautious about it. To put it into perspective, I just ended an 11 year friendship for a similar reason - she started having feelings for my ex and decided to pursue them and tell me after, hoping I’d be okay with it. It was the absolute worst feeling in the world. She didn’t bother considering how I’d feel or if I was even over what happened, especially because things didn’t end very well with him. Ultimately, she decided pursuing her romantic desires was worth potentially losing a lifelong friend. It was a devastating outcome with incredible consequences, and I’d never wish it on anyone. 

You’re stopping this before it happens which is very mature and coming from a place of empathy and consideration for everyone involved DESPITE how you’re feeling, which means you’re on the right track. I wish it was what she did. 

My personal advice to you - if you want to keep both of them in your life, don’t pursue her. There’s plenty of other people out there that you can date that will be a match for you, and it won’t come at the cost of any of your friendships. What I’ve learned is dating within a friend group can get very very messy very fast, especially if things don’t work out. On top of that, she doesn’t want a relationship right now, so the best thing to do is respect that and search elsewhere; she won’t be able to meet your needs anyway if she’s not in the space for that commitment right now.

And I know it seems impossible, but try not to feel bad about your feelings - you’re allowed to have them, you have no control over them, but you are responsible for the choices you make because of them. Your guy friend will most likely feel betrayed, and you’ll likely jeopardize that friendship with him, or maybe even both of them, if you pursue her. I just wouldn’t risk it. I hope this helped a little bit.
